extracted.intended_audience: law students, legal scholars, and practitioners studying English constitutional, territorial, and public law (Blackstone's Commentaries)
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of the territorial composition, jurisdictional rules, and constitutional arrangements of the British crown and its dominions (England, Scotland, Ireland, Man, Channel Islands, plantations), with ecclesiastical and civil territorial subdivisions. Useful for understanding which laws apply where and the structural limits of authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article 1 — Union into Great Britain
rubrics_metrics.description: On the first of May 1707, and for ever after, the kingdoms of England and Scotland shall be united into one kingdom, by the name of Great Britain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the foundational stipulation effecting political union; subsequent articles regulate succession, representation, and preservation of certain institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article 2 — Succession
rubrics_metrics.description: The succession to the monarchy of Great Britain shall be the same as was before settled with regard to that of England.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establishes continuity of dynastic succession rules from England to the new united kingdom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article 3 — Single Parliament
rubrics_metrics.description: The united kingdom shall be represented by one parliament.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unifies legislative representation; affects how statutes and parliamentary authority operate across former separate kingdoms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article 4 — Communication of Rights and Privileges
rubrics_metrics.description: There shall be a communication of all rights and privileges between the subjects of both kingdoms, except where it is otherwise agreed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subjects of both former kingdoms generally share rights unless specific exceptions are stipulated elsewhere in the union terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article 9 — Apportionment of Land Tax
rubrics_metrics.description: When England raises 2,000,000_l._ by a land tax, Scotland shall raise 48,000_l._
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies proportional fiscal burdens/arrangements between England and Scotland as part of the union's financial provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Articles 16 & 17 — Standardization of Coin, Weights, and Measures
rubrics_metrics.description: The standards of the coin, of weights, and of measures, shall be reduced to those of England, throughout the united kingdoms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imposes economic/metric uniformity across the united realm, aligning Scottish standards to English ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article 18 — Trade, Customs, Excise; Protection of Scottish Private Rights
rubrics_metrics.description: The laws relating to trade, customs, and the excise, shall be the same in Scotland as in England. But all the other laws of Scotland shall remain in force; but alterable by the parliament of Great Britain. Yet with this caution; that laws relating to public policy are alterable at the discretion of the parliament; laws relating to private rights are not to be altered but for the evident utility of the people of Scotland.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes commercial/statutory harmonization from retention of Scottish municipal law, while imposing a constitutional constraint: public policy may be altered broadly but private rights only for evident utility of Scots.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article 22 — Representation of Scottish Peerage & Commons
rubrics_metrics.description: Sixteen peers are to be chosen to represent the peerage of Scotland in parliament, and forty five members to sit in the house of commons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sets precise representation numbers for Scotland in the unified Parliament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article 23 — Privileges and Ranking of Scottish Peers
rubrics_metrics.description: The sixteen peers of Scotland shall have all privileges of parliament: and all peers of Scotland shall be peers of Great Britain, and rank next after those of the same degree at the time of the union, and shall have all privileges of peers, except sitting in the house of lords and voting on the trial of a peer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Details the status, privileges, and limitations attaching to Scottish peers post-union.

rubrics_metrics.name: Union — Fundamental and Essential Conditions (Preservation of Churches and Acts of Uniformity)
rubrics_metrics.description: The preservation of the two churches, of England and Scotland, in the same state that they were in at the time of the union, and the maintenance of the acts of uniformity which establish our common prayer, are expressly declared to be 'fundamental and essential conditions of the union.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alteration of either church's constitution or of the Church of England's liturgy would be an infringement of the union and could endanger it; these religious arrangements are treated as constitutional safeguards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scottish Municipal Law Post-Union
rubrics_metrics.description: The municipal laws of Scotland are ordained to be still observed in that part of the island, unless altered by parliament; and, as the parliament has not yet thought proper, except in a few instances, to alter them, they still (with regard to the particulars unaltered) continue in full force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: English municipal/common law is generally of no force in Scotland; Scottish laws continue unless and until Parliament of Great Britain alters them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statute Interpretation — 'England' to include Wales and Berwick
rubrics_metrics.description: It was declared by statute 20 Geo. II. c. 42. that where England only is mentioned in any act of parliament, the same notwithstanding shall be deemed to comprehend the dominion of Wales, and town of Berwick upon Tweed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarifies statutory scope: references to 'England' may, by statute, be read to include adjacent dominions or towns for purposes of application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Berwick upon Tweed — Jurisdictional Exception
rubrics_metrics.description: The town of Berwick upon Tweed... is not part of the kingdom of England, nor subject to the common law; though it is subject to all acts of parliament, being represented by burgesses therein. And therefore... the general law there used is the Scots law, and the ordinary process of the courts of Westminster-hall is there of no authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anomalous territorial status: subject to statutes and parliamentary representation but governed in practice by Scots law rather than English common law; Westminster process lacks authority there.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ireland — Dependent Distinct Kingdom
rubrics_metrics.description: Ireland is still a distinct kingdom; though a dependent, subordinate kingdom... The inhabitants of Ireland are, for the most part, descended from the English... and as Ireland thus conquered, planted, and governed, still continues in a state of dependence, it must necessarily conform to, and be obliged by such laws as the superior state thinks proper to prescribe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treats Ireland as constitutionally distinct but subordinate; the superior state's laws may bind Ireland by virtue of conquest/dependence subject to statutory and historical qualifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abolition of Brehon Law & Imposition of English Law
rubrics_metrics.description: At Kilkenny, 40 Edw. III, the Brehon law was formally abolished... earlier letters patent and statutes attempted to ordain that Ireland should be governed by the laws of England.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical process of supplanting native Irish law with English law; Blackstone notes resistance and staggered enforcement over centuries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of English Statutes in Ireland — Need for Specific Naming or General Words
rubrics_metrics.description: No acts of the English parliament, since the twelfth of king John, extended into that kingdom; unless it were specially named, or included under general words, such as, 'within any of the king's dominions.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only English statutes that specifically name Ireland or use sufficiently general territorial language bind Ireland; otherwise, separate Irish parliamentary acts govern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poynings' Law — Procedure for Irish Bills
rubrics_metrics.description: 1. The lord lieutenant and council of Ireland must certify to the king under the great seal of Ireland the acts proposed to be passed. 2. The king and council of England are to consider, approve, alter, or reject the said acts; and certify them back again under the great seal of England. 3. They are to be proposed, received, or rejected in the parliament of Ireland.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under Poynings' law the Irish parliament's legislative initiative was tightly controlled by the English crown/council; the Irish parliament had mostly a negative power rather than independent legislative initiative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice of Framing Bills as Heads
rubrics_metrics.description: Bills are often framed in either house of parliament under the denomination of heads for a bill or bills; and in that shape they are offered to the consideration of the lord lieutenant and privy council, who then reject them at pleasure, without transmitting them to England.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes a later practical modification to Poynings' procedure allowing some local drafting but still subject to executive/local veto.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal Scope Rule from 10 Hen. VII
rubrics_metrics.description: By the statute in the 10 Hen. VII. it was enacted, among other things, that all acts of parliament before made in England, should be of force within the realm of Ireland... but no acts of the English parliament made since the 10 Hen. VII. do now bind the people of Ireland, unless specially named or included under general words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes which historical English statutes were imported into Ireland by that statute versus later English statutes which require express inclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foundational Ground of Superiority — Right of Conquest
rubrics_metrics.description: The original and true ground of this superiority is the right of conquest: a right allowed by the law of nations... and founded upon a compact either expressly or tacitly made between the conqueror and the conquered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blackstone articulates the legal rationale for dependence: conquest + tacit compact justify superior state's legal imposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statute 6 Geo. I c.5 — Parliamentary Power Over Ireland
rubrics_metrics.description: By statute 6 Geo. I. c. 5. it is declared, that the kingdom of Ireland ought to be subordinate to, and dependent upon, the imperial crown of Great Britain... and that the king's majesty, with the consent of the lords and commons of Great Britain in parliament, hath power to make laws to bind the people of Ireland.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A later statutory assertion of parliamentary sovereignty over Ireland, modifying prior constitutional relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeals from Ireland to English Courts and Lords
rubrics_metrics.description: The ultimate resort from the courts of justice in Ireland is, as in Wales, to those in England; a writ of error (in the nature of an appeal) lying from the king's bench in Ireland to the king's bench in England... and the appeal from all other courts in Ireland lies immediately to the house of lords here.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit appellate channels to English superior courts ensure legal uniformity and supervisory control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale for Appeals to Superior State Courts
rubrics_metrics.description: The propriety, and even necessity, in all inferior dominions, of this constitution, 'that, though justice be in general administered by courts of their own, yet that the appeal in the last resort ought to be to the courts of the superior state,' is founded upon two reasons: 1. To prevent insensible change of law in the inferior dominion; 2. To prevent judgments adverse to the superiority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Articulates policy reasons for appellate oversight from the superior state's courts over dependent jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Isle of Man — Separate Territory & Statutory Application
rubrics_metrics.description: The isle of Man is a distinct territory from England and is not governed by our laws; neither doth any act of parliament extend to it, unless it be particularly named therein; and then an act of parliament is binding there.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Isle of Man has its own historical jurisdiction; parliamentary acts bind it only by express naming; appeals lay to the king in council; certain landed property and ecclesiastical patronage retained by private families initially but subsequently subject to Crown regulation (e.g., customs/excise).

rubrics_metrics.name: Channel Islands — Ducheal Customs & Limited Parliamentary Reach
rubrics_metrics.description: The islands of Jersey, Guernsey, Sark, Alderney... are governed by their own laws, which are for the most part the ducal customs of Normandy... The king's writ, or process from the courts of Westminster, is there of no force; but his commission is. They are not bound by common acts of our parliaments, unless particularly named.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Channel Islands retain distinct Norman-derived legal systems; domestic English writs lack force though royal commissions and express statutes can apply; appeal lies to the king in council.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of Plantations/Colonies (Occupancy vs Conquest/Cession)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plantations, or colonies in distant countries, are either such where the lands are claimed by right of occupancy only... or where, when already cultivated, they have been either gained by conquest, or ceded to us by treaties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal origin of a colony determines the initial applicable law and the power of the crown to alter local laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule for Newly Planted (Uninhabited) Colonies
rubrics_metrics.description: If an uninhabited country be discovered and planted by English subjects, all the English laws are immediately there in force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where settlers occupy terra nullius, English law accompanies them by way of birthright and carries immediate applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule for Conquered or Ceded Colonies
rubrics_metrics.description: In conquered or ceded countries, that have already laws of their own, the king may indeed alter and change those laws; but, till he does actually change them, the antient laws of the country remain, unless such as are against the law of God, as in the case of an infidel country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Existing legal systems survive post-acquisition until and unless the sovereign deliberately replaces them, subject to moral/Christian law caveats in the period's terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: American Plantations — Status & Parliamentary Control
rubrics_metrics.description: Our American plantations are principally of this latter sort... the common law of England, as such, has no allowance or authority there; they being no part of the mother country, but distinct (though dependent) dominions. They are subject however to the control of the parliament; though (like Ireland, Man, and the rest) not bound by any acts of parliament, unless particularly named.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: American colonies are treated as dependent with local laws and assemblies; governors appointed by the crown; appeals to king in council; statute 7 & 8 W. III. c. 22. declares plantation usages repugnant to laws relative to plantations void.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statute 7 & 8 W. III. c.22 — Repugnancy in Plantations
rubrics_metrics.description: That all laws, by-laws, usages, and customs, which shall be in practice in any of the plantations, repugnant to any law, made or to be made in this kingdom relative to the said plantations, shall be utterly void and of none effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parliamentary enactments concerning plantations prevail over conflicting local customs/usages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign Continental Possessions (e.g., Hanover) — Separate Legal Sphere
rubrics_metrics.description: Any foreign dominions which may belong to the person of the king by hereditary descent, by purchase, or other acquisition, as the territory of Hanover... do not in any wise appertain to the crown of these kingdoms, they are entirely unconnected with the laws of England, and do not communicate with this nation in any respect whatsoever.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personal possessions of the monarch abroad are legally distinct and not subject to English law; political practice (Act of Settlement) contains conditional clauses limiting obligations to defend such dominions without parliamentary consent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Main or High Seas — Admiralty Jurisdiction & Common Law
rubrics_metrics.description: The main or high seas are part of the realm of England, for thereon our courts of admiralty have jurisdiction, as will be shewn hereafter; but they are not subject to the common law. This main sea begins at the low-water-mark.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Admiralty, not common law, governs high-seas matters; territorial demarcation begins at low-water mark.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divisum Imperium Between High- and Low-Water Marks
rubrics_metrics.description: Between the high-water-mark, and the low-water-mark, where the sea ebbs and flows, the common law and the admiralty have divisum imperium, an alternate jurisdiction; one upon the water, when it is full sea; the other upon the land, when it is an ebb.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides a rule allocating jurisdiction between common law courts and admiralty depending on tidal state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ecclesiastical Territorial Division — Provinces to Parishes
rubrics_metrics.description: The ecclesiastical division is, primarily, into two provinces, those of Canterbury and York... Each diocese is divided into archdeaconries... every deanry is divided into parishes. A PARISH is that circuit of ground in which the souls under the care of one parson or vicar do inhabit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sets the hierarchical structure of ecclesiastical jurisdiction and defines a parish as the unit for pastoral care and tithes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tithes — Appropriation and King as Trustee for Extraparochial Tithes
rubrics_metrics.description: Originally tithes could be paid to any priest; later by law primary tithes were to be given to the primariae ecclesiae (mother church). Some lands were never united to any parish (extraparochial) and their tithes are by immemorial custom payable to the king instead of the bishop, in trust that he will distribute them for the general good of the church.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes evolution of tithe law: appropriation to churches, exceptions for private chapels (one-third tithes if cemetery), and the special treatment of extraparochial tithes payable to the Crown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil Territorial Division — Tithings, Hundreds, Counties
rubrics_metrics.description: The civil division of the territory of England is into counties, of those counties into hundreds, of those hundreds into tithings or towns. Tithings (ten families) compose towns/vills; ten tithings make a hundred; an indefinite number of hundreds form a county or shire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the classic Saxon-based administrative divisions and their officers (tithing-man/headborough, hundred court, sheriff/shire-reeve) and variants (wapentakes, lathes, rapes, ridings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Town/City/Borough Distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Towns or vills originally each had a church and were the unit of tithings; a city is a town that is or has been the see of a bishop; a borough is a town that sends burgesses to parliament; many towns are neither city nor borough.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal distinctions affect privileges, governance, and representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hundreds and Wapentakes — Composition and Officers
rubrics_metrics.description: As ten families made up a town, so ten tithings composed a hundred. The hundred is governed by an high constable or bailiff, and formerly there was regularly held in it the hundred court... In some northern counties these hundreds are called wapentakes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes the intermediate local units and their officers/courts; many hundred functions have fallen into disuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counties Palatine — Chester, Durham, Lancaster (Jura Regalia)
rubrics_metrics.description: Three counties, Chester, Durham, and Lancaster, are called counties palatine... because the owners thereof... had jura regalia, as fully as the king hath in his palace; regalem potestatem in omnibus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counties palatine historically enjoyed royal privileges and near-sovereign jurisdiction within the county; legal consequences include largely autonomous administration subject to prescription or specific grants.
